title: Brief it like a professional
desc: Write the specification an AI builder — or a colleague — could build from unaided.
learningGoal: After this lesson the learner can write an automation brief precise enough to be built without a single follow-up question.

steps.title: Most failed builds are failed briefs
steps.bodyMd:
Pieter runs procurement at Van Dijk Groep, an installation firm of sixty people. He asks for **"automate my invoices"** and gets back a routine that reads the wrong mailbox, files nothing, and tells nobody.

The builder was not stupid. It was guessing.

Everything you have learned so far — triggers, steps, the canvas, the dry-run — is downstream of one sentence: **what did you ask for?** A routine can only be as precise as the description it was built from. That is true whether the builder is the assistant beside the canvas or the colleague sitting next to you.

This chapter is about that sentence.

steps.title: Four parts, no exceptions
steps.bodyMd:
Every buildable brief answers four questions, in any order:

1. **When does it start?** A clock time, an inbound event, a form submission, a button. This becomes the trigger.
2. **What does it read?** The app, the table, the mailbox, the form. This becomes the first real step.
3. **What does it decide?** The rule with a number in it, and what the AI should actually produce. This becomes the conditions and the AI step.
4. **What does it produce, and for whom?** The document, the row, the message — and the person or table it reaches. This becomes the last step.

Weak: *"automate my invoices"*. Strong: *"When an invoice mail arrives with a PDF, pull out supplier, number and total; anything over 2500 euro goes to Pieter for approval first; then save the row in the inkoopfacturen table."*

steps.title: Which part is missing?
steps.instruction: Each brief below is missing exactly one of the four parts. Match it to the part that is absent.

pairs.left: "Every Monday at 08:00, have AI write a five-bullet pipeline briefing and e-mail it to Jeroen."
pairs.note: Briefing built from what? Until you name the offertes table, the builder has to invent a source.

pairs.left: "Read the open quotes in the offertes table, write a five-bullet briefing, and e-mail it to Jeroen."
pairs.note: Every routine has exactly one trigger. With no moment named the job reads as on-demand work, so the builder wires a manual button — and it never runs on its own.

pairs.left: "When an invoice mail lands, read the PDF and handle the big ones differently, then save the row in inkoopfacturen."
pairs.note: "The big ones" is not a rule anyone can draw. A condition needs a number and a branch: over 2500 euro goes to approval, the rest goes straight through.

pairs.left: "Every Friday at 16:00, read the closed deals from the offertes table and have AI write a five-bullet summary."
pairs.note: A summary that reaches nobody is a run with a nice output pane. Name the notification, the mailbox or the table.

steps.question: Which detail can the builder — assistant or colleague — never work out for you?

choices.label: The exact name of the table, mailbox or person the result must reach.
The order the steps should run in.
choices.feedback: Mostly it can, from the sentence itself — and that is the point. Sequencing is the builder's job, so spend your words on the facts only you hold.

choices.label: How many steps the routine should end up with.
choices.feedback: Step count is an outcome, not an input. A brief that specifies "six steps" is describing a diagram instead of a job.

choices.label: Which model each AI step should use.
choices.feedback: You rarely need to say. An AI step's model tier sits under Advanced and defaults to auto, and Extract data has no model picker at all — it runs on the one extraction model an admin configured.

steps.explanation: Structure is inferable; facts are not. Nobody else knows that your table is called inkoopfacturen and that Pieter approves anything over 2500 euro. Spend your brief on the nouns.

steps.title: Use the real nouns
steps.bodyMd:
A brief improves fastest when you replace every generic word with the name it has in your workspace.

| Vague | Buildable |
|---|---|
| "our CRM" | the **offertes** datatable |
| "the team" | Jeroen, sales lead — notification plus e-mail |
| "recent quotes" | rows where status is `open` |
| "a summary" | five bullets, each naming a deal and its value |

The names are not decoration. You pick the table from a list and the step keeps a link to the one you chose — so a table that has been deleted, or one this routine may not read, fails the step loudly instead of quietly returning nothing.

Same rule for people: an approver must be a colleague or a group in your organisation. Naming somebody outside it is a save error, on purpose.

steps.title: Say what happens when there is nothing
steps.bodyMd:
The sentence most briefs are missing is the boring one: **what should happen on a quiet week?**

Spell out the edge:

- *"Skip the briefing entirely when no quotes are open."*
- *"If the PDF has no total, stop with an error rather than saving a blank row."*
- *"Only the first twenty-five rows — never the whole table."*

That last one is not fussiness. A list step refuses more than 10,000 items outright, a Datatable read is capped at 1,000 rows, and an Extract data step takes at most 30 fields. A brief that names its own limits produces a routine that degrades politely instead of failing at three in the morning.

And name the destination twice if it matters: on success **and** on failure.

steps.title: Your brief, as a graph
steps.instruction: Here is a finished brief from Van Dijk Groep. Pick the trigger it describes, then assemble only the steps it actually asks for.

scenarios.brief: "Every Monday at 08:00 Amsterdam time, read the open quotes from the offertes table, keep only the first twenty-five rows, have AI write a five-bullet briefing naming the deals at risk, and send it to Jeroen as a notification and an e-mail."

options.label: On form submission
options.desc: Publish a form; every submission runs this

options.label: On a schedule
options.desc: Run at a fixed time, over and over

options.label: On webhook call
options.desc: Run when an HTTP request arrives

options.label: On app event
options.desc: Run when something happens in a connected app

feedback.manual: A button means somebody has to remember. "Every Monday at 08:00" is a clock, and a clock is the Schedule trigger — which also lets you set Europe/Amsterdam and preview the next firing times before you save.
feedback.form: Nobody submits anything here. A form trigger publishes a public page and runs once per submission; this brief names a time, not a submitter.
feedback.webhook: A webhook waits for an outside system to call in with a signed request. Nothing outside is calling — the calendar is.
feedback.app_event: App event fires when something happens in a connected app, such as a new mail. "Every Monday" is not an event in an app; it is a moment on a clock.

palette.label: Shorten list — keep only the first twenty-five
AI step — write the five-bullet briefing

feedback.approve: The brief never asks anyone to decide anything — it asks for a briefing to be sent. An approval pauses the run until a person answers, which would leave Monday's briefing sitting in a queue.
feedback.formpage: A form page pauses the run and shows the next page on the routine's own form link — so it needs a Form trigger. On a scheduled routine the palette shows it disabled for exactly that reason.

steps.title: Your turn: brief your next routine
steps.instruction: Write the brief for a routine you would genuinely use — four or five sentences, plain language, no jargon. Name when it starts, what it reads (by its real name: the app, table, mailbox or form), what it does with what it finds including any rule with a number in it, and where the result lands and who is told. Add the quiet-week sentence if there is one. The AI coach scores it against what a builder would need to build it with no follow-up questions.
steps.placeholder: e.g. Every weekday at 08:30, read yesterday's new rows from the meldingen table where status is open, have AI group them by theme and draft a digest with the top three issues, and send it to Marieke as a notification and an e-mail. Skip the digest entirely when there are no new rows.

steps.question: You hand your brief to Build with AI. The canvas starts narrating "Added 3 steps" and you spot a wrong address on one of them. You click that node. What happens?

choices.label: Nothing — you are told editing is paused until the builder finishes its turn, then you fix it.
Your change is merged into what the assistant is writing.
choices.feedback: Two writers on one definition means whoever saves last wins silently. The lock exists precisely so your edit is not quietly overwritten mid-build.

choices.label: The build is cancelled and you start again from your brief.
choices.feedback: Nothing is thrown away. The turn runs to the end, the canvas is yours again, and everything the assistant placed is editable by hand.

steps.explanation: While the assistant builds, edits are locked — "The AI is building this routine — editing is paused until it finishes." Wait for the turn to end, then either chat another instruction or open the node and correct it yourself.

steps.title: Handing the brief over
steps.bodyMd:
In Studio → **Automations**, press **+** and a fresh draft opens. Its empty canvas says *"Or describe the routine:"* next to an **Assistant** button; press it and a chat box opens beside the canvas. Paste your brief there and send it.

The canvas then narrates itself — **"Added 4 steps"**, **"Reviewing the routine…"** — and usually runs a dry-run on its own before finishing with something like **"Built · 9 steps · 1m 12s"**.

Two things worth knowing:

- Want a starting point? While the chat is still empty, **"Build with the assistant"** offers a few suggested prompts; each one fills the chat box with text you can edit into your own brief. It never sends on its own.
- A routine the assistant has finished is **still a draft**. A person presses **Activate**, and nothing fires until they do.

steps.question: Your brief said "save the invoice row in inkoopfacturen". The assistant builds it; after two live runs the same supplier invoice sits in the table twice. Which sentence was missing from your brief?

choices.label: Whether an existing row should be updated instead of added — and which column identifies it.
The table name — you should have said which datatable to write to.
choices.feedback: You did name it, and the step keeps a link to the table you picked. A correctly named table that collects duplicates is not a naming problem.

choices.label: The trigger — you should have asked for a schedule rather than an inbound mail.
choices.feedback: The trigger decides when the routine wakes up, not how it writes. A scheduled version reading the same mailbox would append the second copy just as happily.

choices.label: The number in the rule — "over 2500 euro" was too vague to act on.
choices.feedback: That threshold decides which invoices need an approval first. Both branches still end at the same write step, so it cannot explain a duplicate row.

steps.explanation: Ambiguity never stops a build — it gets resolved by whoever builds, and their default silently becomes your behaviour. A Datatable "Add or update a row" step only updates when its match column is mapped; unmapped, every run appends. Write the sentence yourself: "update the row with the same invoice number, otherwise add it."

steps.title: Build from your own brief
steps.instruction: Open Automations, press + for a new automation, then press Assistant on the empty canvas and paste the brief you just wrote into the chat box. Let the assistant finish, read what it placed, then press Dry-run. Collapse this lesson while you work — it keeps checking.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
You have finished **Automate Your Week**. You can now:

- **Write a brief in four parts** — when it starts, what it reads, what it decides, what it produces and for whom — and spot which part a weak brief is missing.
- **Use the real nouns**: the table, the mailbox, the person, the threshold with a number in it, and the sentence about the quiet week.
- **Hand it to a builder and check the result** — read what was placed, dry-run it, fix the node yourself, and press Activate when the shape is right.

The habit worth keeping: write the brief before you open the canvas. If you cannot say the job in four sentences, the routine is not ready to be drawn.

ex-automation-brief.title: Brief an automation
ex-automation-brief.task: Describe an automation you would actually use, in plain English: when it should run, what data it reads, what should happen with it including any rule, and where the result lands and who is told.
criteria: Names a concrete trigger — a clock time, an inbound event, a form submission or a button, not just "automatically"
Names the source specifically: the app, table, mailbox or form the routine reads, ideally by its real name
Describes the work specifically enough to act on — the steps, a condition with an actual threshold, or what the AI should produce
States where the result lands and who is told, by name or by role
ex-automation-brief.guidance: Reward a brief a builder could implement without follow-up questions. "Automate my reports" and any brief missing the trigger, the source or the destination must score below pass. A condition stated without a number ("the big ones") loses the third criterion but is not an automatic fail. Handling for the empty case is a plus, not a requirement. Do not reward canvas jargon or step counts in place of facts.

practiceTopic.title: Briefing an automation
practiceTopic.summary: How to describe a routine precisely enough that an AI builder or a colleague can build it without asking a single follow-up question.
facts: A buildable brief answers four questions: when it starts, what it reads, what it decides, and what it produces and for whom.

The + in Studio → Automations opens a new draft; its empty canvas reads "Or describe the routine:" with an Assistant button that opens the builder's chat beside the canvas, where an empty chat offers a few suggested prompts that fill the chat box.
While the assistant builds, editing is paused: "The AI is building this routine — editing is paused until it finishes."
A routine the assistant has finished is still a draft; a person presses Activate before anything fires.
The Schedule trigger defaults to the Europe/Amsterdam timezone and previews the next run times before you save.
An AI step's model tier sits under Advanced and defaults to auto; Extract data has no model picker and uses the one extraction model an admin configured.
Limits worth naming in a brief: a Datatable read is capped at 1,000 rows, list steps refuse more than 10,000 items, and Extract data takes at most 30 fields.
A Datatable "Add or update a row" step only updates when its match column is mapped; leave it unmapped and every run appends a new row instead.

actionChecks.label: Build a routine from your own brief
actionChecks.hint: In Studio → Automations, press +, open the Assistant beside the canvas, paste your brief, let it finish, then press Dry-run.

endpoints.returns: { automations: [...] } — every routine owned by the caller, with id, title, triggerType, isDraft, isActive, createdAt, updatedAt
{ runs: [...] } — the caller's runs across all routines, each with automationId, mode ('live' or 'dry_run') and status

criteria.label: A second routine of your own exists
criteria.hint: Chapter 5 built your first one. This step wants a second, built from the brief you just wrote.

criteria.label: You dry-ran it
criteria.hint: Press Dry-run in the builder header — it previews every step and performs no real actions.
criteria.rule: runs contains a row with mode == 'dry_run' whose automationId equals the id of the most recently created automation
